title: How to Grow Past Senior Engineer
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Gregor Ojstersek lays out four concrete tactics for engineers stuck at the Senior level, opening with his own admission that he stagnated because he never told his manager what direction he wanted his career to go, relying instead on luck and accumulated credibility to eventually earn a Team Lead role. His first and most emphasized tactic is proactively naming career goals to a manager in a 1:1 rather than waiting to be noticed, illustrated by his own move from leading one team to three after directly asking his former manager's manager for the opening role. He then details a 'brag list' practice for tracking achievements against explicit goals, arguing a manager sees only about 40% of an engineer's actual work and that the practice also counters impostor syndrome by making a self-taught engineer's real progress visible over time. The remaining two tactics describe becoming the recognized 'go-to' person for a specific project, domain, or technology through proactive learning, and proposing and personally leading an unassigned but impactful improvement, both framed as ways to demonstrate readiness for the next title before formally receiving it. The piece closes by reiterating that impact and ownership should precede permission, not follow it.
points: Reframes the common career-stagnation complaint as a communication failure rather than a recognition failure, using the author's own stalled post-Senior period (caused by never stating a direction to his manager) as the diagnostic example.

Introduces the specific practical mechanism of a 'brag list,' justified by the concrete claim that a manager sees only about 40% of an engineer's actual work, making self-tracked achievement documentation necessary rather than optional for promotion conversations.

Ties the brag-list practice directly to countering impostor syndrome, using the author's own self-taught-engineer background to show how a written achievement record reveals a pattern of strength (in his case, collaboration and expectation-management) that pointed toward a specific career path.

Defines the 'go-to person' status operationally as being the recognized authority for a specific project, domain, or technology, achieved through proactive skill acquisition ahead of organizational need, using a concrete Angular-migration example.

States plainly that promotion follows demonstrated impact rather than preceding it, and specifies the exact mechanics of proposing an unassigned improvement: do quick fixes immediately, escalate larger ones to a manager or lead, and always volunteer to own the implementation.
quotes: After I became a Senior Software Engineer, I didn't know exactly what my next step would be. I wasn't very convincing to my manager in 1:1 meetings about what my career would look like in the future. So I was stagnating in my career, feeling like I hit a wall.
If they don't know about your goals and how you wish to grow, they won't be able to put you in a position to showcase your skills. What you say is important, but so is how you say it.
Your manager only sees about 40% of the work that you do, so it's important to let them know about all the great things you do that they might not know about.

I am a self-taught engineer, and at the beginning of my career, I thought that university graduates must all have amazing programming skills and that I would never be able to get to their level. A brag list would have helped me to see that progress.
This learning made me the most knowledgeable engineer in my organization on Angular, which automatically made me the go-to person. Everyone was coming to me with questions and issues
Engineers who truly stand out are the ones who find impactful work to do without being asked, then take ownership to execute and implement it as well.

The key is not to wait until someone gives you permission to operate at the next level. Start creating impact beyond your own work. Take ownership of problems that nobody explicitly assigned to you. The title usually comes after you've already shown you can operate at that level.
